concept.name: LSM-Tree Compaction Strategies: Size-Tiered vs. Leveled vs. FIFO
concept.title: LSM-Tree Compaction Strategies: Size-Tiered vs. Leveled vs. FIFO
concept.tagline: Navigating the RUM Conjecture trade-off between Read, Write, and Space Amplification in LSM storage engines.
concept.purpose: Understand how Size-Tiered (STCS), Leveled (LCS), and FIFO compaction shape SSD wear, disk headroom, and point/range read latency in RocksDB, Cassandra, and Pebble.

prerequisites.title: B-Tree vs. LSM-Tree
prerequisites.summary: Know that LSM-Trees turn random writes into sequential MemTable flushes to immutable SSTables, which later require background compaction.

prerequisites.title: Bloom Filters
prerequisites.summary: Understand how per-SSTable Bloom filters avoid disk reads for keys absent from a file.

spark.summary: Size-Tiered Compaction minimizes write amplification (~10x) at the cost of 50% temporary disk headroom and multi-file reads, while Leveled Compaction caps space overhead at ~1.1x and bounds read amplification via non-overlapping key ranges.
spark.keyTakeaway: When choosing an LSM compaction strategy, pick Leveled Compaction for read-heavy or disk-constrained workloads, Size-Tiered Compaction for write-heavy ingestion with ample SSD headroom, and FIFO only for TTL-expiring time-series logs.
spark.byteSummary:
An LSM-Tree buffers writes in a MemTable and flushes immutable SSTables sequentially—giving blazing-fast writes, until unmerged files pile up and force reads to check dozens of SSTables. Compaction merges those SSTables in the background, but the RUM Conjecture proves you cannot minimize Read, Update/Write, and Memory/Space Amplification simultaneously.

Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS, Cassandra's classic default) groups similar-sized SSTables and merges 4 of them into one larger tier. It keeps write amplification low (~10x), but because files within a tier have overlapping key ranges, point reads must check every tier—and compacting the largest tier temporarily needs 50% free disk space.

Leveled Compaction (LCS, RocksDB's default) organizes levels L1, L2, L3... with a 10x size ratio where every SSTable inside a level has strictly non-overlapping key ranges. That caps space amplification at ~1.1x and lets point reads binary-search at most one SSTable per level, at the cost of ~25–35x write amplification as keys get rewritten down each level.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & The Uncompacted SSTable Pileup
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows why uncompacted LSM flushes destroy read latency and leak deleted disk space.

explanation.foundation: Every MemTable flush creates a brand-new immutable SSTable on disk. Over a day of writes, an engine can flush hundreds of overlapping SSTables.
explanation.core: Without compaction, a `GET(key)` or range scan must merge-iterate across all 500 SSTables, and overwrites or tombstones (`DELETE`) never reclaim disk space. Yet running compaction greedily on every flush rewrites gigabytes of cold data repeatedly—burning out NVMe SSD endurance.
explanation.deepDive: This three-way tension is formalized as the RUM Conjecture: Read Amplification (files checked per lookup), Write Amplification (bytes written to SSD / logical bytes written), and Space Amplification (total disk bytes / logical live dataset size).

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: Size-Tiered vs. Leveled Geometry
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Contrasts overlapping size tiers against 10x-ratio non-overlapping levels.

explanation.foundation: In STCS, 4 small 64 MB SSTables merge into one 256 MB SSTable; 4 x 256 MB merge into 1 GB, and so on. Any key can appear in multiple tiers simultaneously.
explanation.core: In LCS, L0 contains freshly flushed overlapping SSTables. Once L0 reaches a threshold (e.g., 4–8 files), it merges into L1 (e.g., 10 MB total), which partitions keys into sorted, non-overlapping SSTables (`[A..D], [E..H], ...`). Each subsequent level `L_i` is 10x larger than `L_{i-1}` (L2 = 100 MB, L3 = 1 GB, L4 = 10 GB).
explanation.deepDive: Because 90% of all data lives in the bottom-most level `L_max` (geometric series `1 + 0.1 + 0.01...`), LCS space amplification stays around `1.11x`—saving up to 45% of SSD capacity on multi-terabyte clusters.

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: Write vs. Space Amplification Math
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Derives why LCS write amplification scales as `O(T * L)` where T=10 is the level fanout ratio.

explanation.foundation: When a 100 MB SSTable from L2 merges down into L3 (1,000 MB), it overlaps with roughly `T = 10` SSTables in L3.
explanation.core: That means moving 100 MB down one level reads and rewrites ~1,000 MB (`T = 10x` write amplification per level). Across 3–4 level transitions, LCS write amplification totals `~30x–40x`, whereas STCS only rewrites each byte once per tier (`~10x`).
explanation.deepDive: FIFO Compaction is a third specialized mode: it never merges SSTables at all! It simply deletes the oldest SSTable file once total size exceeds a cap or TTL expires—achieving `1.0x` write amplification for immutable time-series logs.

codeExample.title: LSM Amplification Estimator (STCS vs. LCS)
codeExample.code:
def estimate_lsm_amplification(level_ratio_T=10, num_levels_L=4):
    # Leveled: worst-case ~ T bytes rewritten per level + WAL/L0
    lcs_write_amp = 1 + (level_ratio_T * (num_levels_L - 1))
    # Space amp: geometric series sum 1 / (1 - 1/T)
    lcs_space_amp = 1.0 / (1.0 - 1.0 / level_ratio_T)
    # Size-Tiered: ~1 rewrite per tier, but up to 50% temp space overhead
    stcs_write_amp = num_levels_L * 2
    stcs_space_amp = 2.0
    return {
        'lcs': {'write_amp': lcs_write_amp, 'space_amp': round(lcs_space_amp, 2)},
        'stcs': {'write_amp': stcs_write_amp, 'space_amp': stcs_space_amp},
    }

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: L0 Pileups, Write Stalls & Hybrid Tiered-Leveled
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Explains why unthrottled compaction causes p99 read spikes and how RocksDB prevents L0 overflow.

explanation.foundation: If client writes arrive faster than background compaction can drain L0 into L1, L0 accumulates dozens of overlapping files.
explanation.core: Once L0 hits a soft limit (e.g., 20 files), RocksDB applies smooth write-stalls (rate-limiting incoming writes) and hard-stops writes at 36 files so read latency doesn't degrade 10x.
explanation.deepDive: Modern engines like RocksDB/Pebble also offer **Universal / Hybrid Compaction** (STCS in upper levels, LCS in bottom levels) to get low write amp on hot recent data while keeping 1.1x space amp on cold data.

decisionFramework.problem: How to pick an LSM compaction strategy that balances SSD endurance, disk headroom, and p99 read latency.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Leave STCS enabled on a read-heavy or 85%-full SSD cluster.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: STCS runs out of disk space during major compactions (needs 50% free headroom) and suffers slow point/range reads across overlapping tiers.
decisionFramework.decision: Default to Leveled Compaction (LCS) for balanced/read-heavy KV workloads, STCS only for write-dominated append workloads with >=50% free disk, and FIFO for pure TTL logs.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: LCS trades ~3x higher SSD write amplification for 1.1x space efficiency and predictable O(L) point reads.

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use LCS
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Identifies delete-tombstone traps, SSD wear limits, and FIFO misuse.

explanation.foundation: Deletes in an LSM-Tree write a tombstone marker—space is NOT freed until compaction reaches the bottom-most level (`L_max`) where the original key lives.
explanation.core: When NOT to use Leveled Compaction: if your workload is 95%+ blind appends/sensor logs with fixed 7-day TTL and zero updates, LCS burns 30x SSD endurance rewriting logs down 4 levels for nothing—use FIFO compaction (`1.0x` write amp) or time-windowed compaction (TWCS) instead!
explanation.deepDive: Assumptions & Limitations: Amplification estimates assume uniform random key distributions (`T=10`, `L=4`). Heavily skewed hot-key overwrites actually *reduce* LCS write amplification because MemTable and L0 deduplicate repeated updates before they ever reach L3. Glossary: Write Amplification (physical SSD bytes / logical bytes), Space Amplification (on-disk size / live data size), Tombstone (deletion marker), VersionEdit (atomic MANIFEST update).

decisionExercise.prompt: A cluster running Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) is at 72% SSD utilization with a single 800 GB Tier-3 SSTable and 3 more 800 GB SSTables about to compact. What happens when compaction triggers?

options.label: Compaction needs ~3.2 TB of temporary space (or at least 50% free disk for the largest tier) and fails with `ENOSPC` (disk full), stalling the node.
options.explanation: Correct! STCS cannot delete input SSTables until the merged output SSTable finishes writing, requiring up to 50% free disk headroom.

options.label: STCS automatically switches to Leveled Compaction mid-merge.
options.explanation: Compaction strategies do not switch automatically on disk pressure.

options.label: Disk usage immediately drops to 30% before writing.
options.explanation: Old SSTables remain on disk until the new merged file is atomically committed.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does Leveled Compaction (LCS) with a level size ratio of `T = 10` keep space amplification near `1.11x`?

options.text: Because ~90% of all data sits in the largest non-overlapping bottom level (`L_max`), leaving only ~10% in upper levels.
options.feedback: Correct! `1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ... = 1.111x`, and non-overlapping ranges minimize stale duplicates.

options.text: Because LCS compresses data with Zstd 10x better than STCS.
options.feedback: Block compression is orthogonal to compaction geometry.

options.text: Because LCS never writes a WAL.
options.feedback: LSM engines always use a WAL for durability.

options.text: Because LCS deletes keys immediately without tombstones.
options.feedback: LCS still uses tombstones until they reach `L_max`.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Geometric 10x level sizing concentrates 90% of data in `L_max`, capping space overhead near 11%.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is FIFO Compaction the best choice over both STCS and LCS?

options.text: For immutable time-series or log data that expires purely by TTL/size cap with no point updates or deletes.
options.feedback: Correct! FIFO drops whole expired SSTables at 1.0x write amplification.

options.text: For bank account balances with frequent overwrites.
options.feedback: Frequent overwrites need STCS or LCS to deduplicate stale versions.

options.text: When point-lookup read latency must be minimized across random keys.
options.feedback: FIFO leaves overlapping files unmerged, hurting random point reads.

options.text: When you need SQL foreign keys.
options.feedback: Compaction strategies do not implement SQL constraints.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: FIFO avoids all compaction I/O by deleting oldest SSTables once retention limits are reached.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does RocksDB enforce soft and hard write-stalls when L0 file count climbs (e.g., 20 and 36 files)?

options.text: To prevent unbounded L0 overlap from ruining point/range read latency and causing memory/disk exhaustion.
options.feedback: Correct! Because L0 files overlap, every uncompacted L0 file adds to read amplification.

options.text: Because Linux filesystems only allow 36 files in a directory.
options.feedback: Filesystems allow millions of files; the limit is for read-path latency.

options.text: To disable Bloom filters during bursts.
options.feedback: Bloom filters remain active; stalls throttle write ingestion.

options.text: To force clients to switch to STCS.
options.feedback: Stalls give LCS background threads time to catch up.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Backpressure via write-stalls keeps read amplification and L0 backlog bounded under sustained write bursts.

beginner.summary: LSM compaction merges flushed files so reads stay fast: Size-Tiered writes less but needs 50% free disk, while Leveled keeps disk tight and reads fast.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When tuning an LSM database, use Leveled Compaction for tight disk space and fast reads, or Size-Tiered for heavy writes with extra SSD space.
beginner.byteSummary: Size-Tiered merges similar-sized files with less SSD wear but needs lots of free disk space. Leveled keeps each level sorted without overlaps so reads check fewer files.

intermediate.summary: Compare STCS (~10x write amp, 2x space amp), LCS (~30x write amp, 1.11x space amp), and FIFO (1x write amp) across the RUM Conjecture.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When choosing an LSM compaction strategy, match LCS to read-heavy/disk-tight KV stores, STCS to write-heavy workloads, and FIFO to TTL logs.
intermediate.byteSummary: STCS minimizes write amplification at ~10x but needs 50% disk headroom; LCS bounds space at 1.11x with non-overlapping key ranges; write-stalls cap L0 overlap.

advanced.summary: Quantitative RUM trade-offs (`WA ~ T*(L-1)`, `SA = 1/(1-1/T)`), L0 write-stall braking, and hybrid Tiered-Leveled compaction for NVMe SSDs.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating multi-TB LSM clusters on NVMe, combine Leveled bottom levels with rate-limited background compaction and L0 write-stalls to protect p99 reads.
advanced.byteSummary: Modeling `WA = 1 + T*(L-1)` and `SA = 1/(1-1/T)` explains why hybrid Universal/Leveled compaction and L0 write-stalls prevent both SSD wear-out and p99 read stalls.
